title: New Grub Street: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: The New Grub Street: Ambition, Poverty, and the Literary Marketplace

utterances.text: Welcome to New Grub Street Unpacked, a close reading of George Gissing's great novel of literary life, ambition, and slow ruin.
Published in 1891, New Grub Street remains one of the most unflinching portraits of what it actually costs to write for a living.
Not what the romantics promised — the garret, the inspiration, the triumph — but the grinding arithmetic of pages and pounds.
To help us unpack this novel — its brilliance, its cruelty, its extraordinary relevance — I have three exceptional guests.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels on audio than perhaps anyone alive.
He comes to Gissing as a performer — hearing the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments written for the voice.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is fundamentally a moral art.
He will keep us honest — and occasionally withering — about the difference between social critique and genuine imaginative literature.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as a document of class power — who gains, who suffers, and why.
For this novel in particular, I suspect he'll have rather a lot to say.
So — New Grub Street.
The title itself is an act of deliberate provocation — the old Grub Street was London's notorious hive of hack writers, and Gissing is asking: what has changed?
Oliver, as someone who has spent his life inhabiting the voices of literary characters — what kind of world does Gissing drop us into on page one?
The first thing that strikes you — and it strikes you immediately — is the sheer material weight of the world Gissing conjures.
Edwin Reardon is introduced to us not in the act of writing but in the act of failing to write.
He is staring at blank pages, counting how many he has managed, doing the dreadful arithmetic of whether he can finish the novel before the rent falls due.
And what Gissing does — which is both cruel and completely honest — is make that arithmetic the drama.
Not the romantic agony of the unfulfilled artist, but the genuinely rather squalid pressure of not having enough money.
And then there is Jasper Milvain, introduced in the same early chapters — Reardon's great contrast.
Jasper looks at the literary marketplace with the cheerful eyes of a man who has decided not to be ashamed of it.
He is going to sell, and sell well, and he sees absolutely no reason to pretend otherwise.
What interests me about that opening — and Oliver has put his finger precisely on it — is that Gissing establishes the moral stakes through character, not through argument.
Reardon and Milvain are not simply representatives of competing economic positions.
They are two recognisable human types — the man who cannot compromise his sense of what is good, and the man who has decided that compromise is simply intelligence.
Gissing is very candid, actually, about Milvain's charm.
He does not make him a villain — he makes him rather likeable, which is the far more disturbing choice.
Because the reader is in perpetual danger of agreeing with Jasper, even while watching what his philosophy produces in the world around him.
Dr. Johnson said that no man but a blockhead ever wrote except for money — Milvain is simply Johnson's maxim given legs and a first-rate social manner.
I want to press on that word 'philosophy,' because I think Milvain's position isn't really a philosophy — it's a diagnosis.

He has looked at the literary marketplace of the 1880s — the three-volume novel collapsing, the cheap periodicals expanding, the reading public being actively manufactured by mass education — and he has simply described what he sees.
Very early in the novel, Milvain tells his sisters — quite breezily — that literature nowadays is a trade.
He says something to the effect that your successful man of letters is not the inspired genius but the man who has learned the trick of the market and works it with industry.
And here is the crucial thing — Gissing gives that speech to the character who survives.
The novel is structured so that Milvain's cynicism is not punished — it is rewarded.
That is not a conservative moral fable about the dangers of compromise — that is a structural analysis of how literary capitalism actually functions.
I would not entirely dispute that — but I think one ought to be careful about what 'rewarded' means in this novel.
Milvain gets the career, yes. He gets Amy. He gets the income.
But Gissing is not celebrating any of that.
The novel ends on a note that I would describe as — exhausted lucidity.
Milvain has won on the market's terms, and those terms are shown to be impoverished ones — aesthetically, humanly, imaginatively.
Can I just say something about the sheer pleasure of reading Milvain — because I think we're in danger of making him sound grim, and he isn't?
He is genuinely funny. He is quick. He has the best lines.
Gissing is a writer who gets far too little credit for his comic invention, and Milvain is the proof.
Part of what makes the novel so devastating is that the man most adapted to his world is also the most alive to it.
Poor Reardon is heroic and admirable and absolutely miserable — and Gissing doesn't let us look away from that.
And that's where I'd locate the real radicalism of the novel — not in any explicit politics, but in the character of Harold Biffen.
Biffen is Reardon's friend — another struggling writer, poorer still, living in near-destitution — who is writing a novel of absolute, uncompromising realism.
He calls it 'Mr. Bailey, Grocer' — a novel about commonplace people in which nothing extraordinary happens.
No one will publish it. No one will read it. And Biffen knows this — and continues anyway.
That is Gissing's most uncomfortable figure — not the man who compromises, not the man who struggles and is defeated, but the man who pursues pure artistic integrity straight off a cliff.
The market doesn't punish Biffen. It simply ignores him. Which is, of course, worse.
Three men — Reardon, Milvain, Biffen — and between them they map virtually every position a writer can occupy in relation to the market.
That structural ambition alone is remarkable — but what makes this novel devastating rather than merely clever is how Gissing embeds that structure in the daily texture of a life.
And at the centre of that daily texture is Edwin Reardon — a man watching his talent, his marriage, and his health erode in almost unbearable slow motion.
In our next segment, we'll look closely at exactly that process — the machinery of Reardon's decline, and how Gissing makes us feel every turn of the screw.

segments.title: The Machinery of Decline: Reardon's Spiral into Obscurity

utterances.text: We've been talking about how the literary marketplace in New Grub Street rewards calculation over art.
Now I want to turn to the figure who pays the highest price for refusing that bargain — Edwin Reardon.
His decline is the novel's great tragic engine, and it is worth examining how precisely Gissing constructs it.
What strikes me first about Reardon is how completely Gissing refuses him any romantic exemption from the grind.
He is not a misunderstood genius rotting in a garret with beautiful contempt for the world.
He is a man sitting in front of a blank page, counting the words he has written that day, and finding them wanting.
Gissing gives us the actual arithmetic of literary failure — pages per day, shillings per thousand words.
It is devastatingly undignified, and that is precisely the point.
I think one must be careful not to reduce Reardon's tragedy to economic mechanism alone.
What Gissing is really examining is a failure of will — and will is a moral category, not merely an economic one.
Reardon knows, with some clarity, what he must do to survive — write the popular thing, compromise the artistic scruple.
He cannot bring himself to do it, and Gissing is honest enough not to make that refusal entirely heroic.
There is something of paralysis in Reardon — an inability to act that is almost Hamlet-like in its texture.
I'd push back on framing this as a failure of will, Sir Edmund, because that makes it a private drama.
What Gissing shows us is how the market actively produces the conditions that make serious work impossible.
Reardon is trapped in a two-room flat in Islington, writing against a deadline imposed by rent and a wife's expectations.
The silence necessary for imaginative work has been colonised by anxiety — and anxiety is not a moral failing, it's a structural condition.
Gissing himself lived this — he knew that poverty doesn't just make writing hard, it makes the mind itself jagged and unworkable.
And what Gissing captures with such terrible fidelity is the specific texture of that creative paralysis.
There's a passage — and I hear it almost as a stage direction — where Reardon sits at his desk and the words simply will not come.
Gissing writes that Reardon's imagination had 'refused to work,' that he 'could not get a single sentence constructed.'
That's not literary metaphor — that is clinical description of the writer's despair, and anyone who has faced a blank page will recognise it instantly.
The brilliance is in the ordinariness of it — no grand operatic crisis, just the grinding failure of a Tuesday afternoon.
And yet — and this is where I think the novel becomes genuinely great — Gissing does not spare Reardon from accountability.
Consider his marriage to Amy. Reardon chose a woman whose appetites were formed by a comfortable middle-class life.
He made that choice in a spirit of romantic optimism quite disconnected from his actual material circumstances.
Gissing shows us — with great precision — that Reardon's fatal error is not artistic but romantic: choosing to believe the world can be otherwise than it is.
Johnson would have said something very sharp about that kind of self-deception, I think.
The marriage is absolutely central, and I think it reveals something that goes beyond individual character judgment.
Amy is not simply a cold woman who abandons her husband — she is a woman formed by a class whose values are material.
Gissing writes of her with this devastating clarity: that she had 'the kind of nature which, in a woman, is seen at its best amid comfortable surroundings.'
Which is to say — she was made for the life Reardon promised and could not deliver.
Their estrangement is not a failure of love — it is the class system working exactly as designed, penetrating even the most intimate space.
What kills me about the Reardon-Amy scenes is the terrible politeness of their disintegration.
They don't have screaming rows — they have these agonising conversations about money, about the novel, about what they might do.
And there's that awful moment when Reardon suggests they revert to poverty together — take a small flat, live simply, let him write without pressure.
It's a beautiful idea — romantic in exactly the way Sir Edmund means, quite disconnected from Amy's reality.
And Amy's rejection of that proposal is, in its quiet way, the hinge on which his entire fate turns.
One must also speak of Biffen in this context — because Biffen is Reardon's shadow, his alternative fate.
Harold Biffen chooses poverty absolutely — he refuses the compromise, lives in conditions of genuine squalor, and writes his realistic novel about the utterly commonplace.
And what does he get for it? The manuscript nearly burns in a lodging-house fire. The book is published and sinks without a trace.
Gissing sets Biffen up as the purest version of the artistic ideal, and then destroys him with almost clinical efficiency.
The novel is quite merciless on this point: integrity, pursued without compromise, leads not to vindication but to oblivion.
Biffen's novel — 'Mr Bailey, Grocer' — is one of the most extraordinary metafictional gestures in Victorian literature.
A novel about the absolute banality of lower-middle-class life, written with complete artistic seriousness, published into indifference.
Gissing is telling us something precise about what the market does: it doesn't only crush bad work — it crushes good work with equal efficiency.
The market is not a meritocracy. It is an apparatus for producing what sells, full stop.
And Biffen's gentle end — his suicide in the open air, thinking of Helen — is the novel's most devastating indictment of that apparatus.
Biffen's end is heartbreaking precisely because it is so undramatic — he slips away almost apologetically.
And Reardon's death has the same quality — he dies of illness, of exhaustion really, back in poverty, having made his hopeless peace with Amy too late.
Gissing gives his heroes no deathbed speeches, no final illuminations — just the body giving out under the accumulated weight of defeat.
That is, in its own way, a kind of formal radicalism — Victorian novels are supposed to mean something at the end.
Gissing insists that for men like Reardon and Biffen, things simply — stop.
What's remarkable is that this unrelenting darkness co-exists in the novel with a very particular kind of comedy — the comedy of the hack, grinding away against all odds.
That's where we're heading next — how Gissing finds something almost farcical in the literature-as-industry machinery, and why it matters.

segments.title: Comic Desperation: Humor and Survival in the Hack's Life

utterances.text: We've been tracing Reardon's tragic spiral — the way failure grinds a sensitive man down to nothing.
But Gissing is not only writing tragedy — there is a dark, mordant comedy running through this novel that deserves its own reckoning.
The hacks, the journalists, the penny-a-liners — they are desperate figures, and yet Gissing finds something grimly, brilliantly funny in their desperation.
This is where I always want to grab people by the lapels and say: read the Whelpdale scenes.
Whelpdale is a figure who fails at absolutely everything he attempts — and yet fails with such magnificent, undefended cheerfulness that you cannot help but adore him.

He turns up at one point having conceived a new literary scheme — I believe it's his fourth or fifth — and he announces it with the full confidence of a man who has never once been chastened by experience.
Gissing gives him this marvellous line about how the reading public doesn't want literature — it wants something to look at on the train.
And you laugh — and then you realise that Whelpdale is absolutely right, and that's where the comedy curdles into something else entirely.
Oliver is quite right to single out Whelpdale, though I'd frame him slightly differently.
Whelpdale is not merely a comic figure — he is a study in a particular kind of resilience that Gissing treats with genuine ambivalence.
The man simply refuses to be destroyed by failure — and in a novel full of men who are destroyed by it, that refusal is not trivial.
Whether that resilience represents a kind of moral shallowness or a genuine adaptive virtue — Gissing leaves that question beautifully open.
Think of how he contrasts with Reardon — who has all the sensitivity and none of the buoyancy.
I want to push back a little on the word 'resilience,' because I think it softens what Gissing is actually showing us.
Whelpdale's cheerfulness isn't a character trait — it's an adaptation to a market that has no use for genuine literary feeling.
The comedy in Whelpdale is the comedy of a man who has correctly read the conditions of his own exploitation and decided to profit from them rather than be crushed by them.
His great project — Chit-Chat, the magazine aimed at people who can only concentrate for two minutes — is Gissing's most savage joke about the commodification of the written word.
And the joke's punchline is that it succeeds.
That's the precise point where the novel's comedy becomes almost unbearable, isn't it.
Gissing describes Chit-Chat as being designed so that nothing in it requires sustained attention — every item snappy, every article brief, every thought pre-digested.
And Whelpdale delivers this vision with the enthusiasm of a man who genuinely believes he has solved the problem of literature.
The comedy is farcical on the surface and absolutely merciless underneath.
It's the kind of joke that leaves a mark.
And Whelpdale isn't the only source of this dark comedy — there's also the whole world of Jasper Milvain's circle, the journalism crowd, the conversations at the Milvain dinner table.
Oliver, is there a particular scene or exchange that captures this comic texture for you?
The conversations between Jasper and his sisters Dora and Maud are something I return to again and again.
There's a marvellous early scene where Jasper is lecturing them on the proper attitude toward literary hackwork — quite without shame, quite without irony on his own part.
He says something to the effect that the struggle for existence among writers is no different from the struggle among costermongers — only the commodity differs.
And he means it as a liberating insight — as if recognising the market frees you from any obligation to feel bad about serving it.
The comedy is that Jasper is perfectly correct in his analysis and perfectly hollow in his soul — and he doesn't notice either fact.
The sisters are essential to understanding what Gissing is doing with comedy in this novel.
Dora and Maud are not merely bystanders to Jasper's brilliant cynicism — they are themselves aspiring writers grinding through the same machinery.
Their situation has a specific comic poignancy — they are educated, they have genuine taste, and they are writing articles for women's magazines about household management.
Gissing is far too honest to present this as merely degrading — there is something he respects in the way they simply get on with it.
But the comedy of the gap between their capacities and their commissions is very precisely rendered.
The Milvain sisters embody something very specific about the gendered economy of literary labour in this period.
Women writers in the 1880s had access to certain markets — the domestic, the sentimental, the instructional — and those markets paid less and were valued less.
Gissing doesn't editorialise about this — he just shows it in the texture of their daily work, the rates they're offered, the subjects they're assigned.
And yet these women survive — which is more than can be said for Reardon, who had the masculine privilege of being taken seriously and was destroyed by it.
That observation cuts deeply — and it connects to something I find genuinely comic and genuinely devastating in equal measure.
There's the figure of Harold Biffen, who is writing what he calls his 'absolutely realistic' novel — a book about a man who is entirely ordinary, doing entirely ordinary things.
Biffen describes his project with total seriousness — this will be the novel that captures true working-class life without sentimentality or condescension.
And he is clearly right — it probably is a serious work of art.
It also has absolutely no chance of being published, read, or noticed by anyone.
Gissing gives Biffen a nobility that is comic in its utter impracticality — and tragic in its utter sincerity.
Biffen is one of the finest minor characters in late Victorian fiction, and he is consistently undervalued.
His dedication to his novel — Mr. Bailey, Grocer, I believe — is presented with complete moral seriousness by Gissing.
There's a scene where his manuscript is nearly destroyed in a fire — he saves it at great personal cost — and the reader is made to feel the full weight of that near-loss.
The comedy is not at Biffen's expense — it is at the world's expense for failing to deserve a Biffen.
The Biffen fire episode is one of the moments where the comedy and the horror are absolutely inseparable.
He lives in genuine poverty — near-starvation, an attic room, inadequate fuel — and the manuscript he's protecting represents years of labour that will never be compensated.
Gissing frames it almost as a set piece — the hapless artist in his garret, the flames, the heroic rescue.
But then he refuses to let you rest in the comedy — you remember what the manuscript is worth in market terms, which is nothing.
The laughter catches in your throat.
That phrase captures something essential about Gissing's comic mode — the laughter that catches in the throat.
He never lets the comedy be comfortable — there's always the economic reality pressing up against the joke and puncturing it.
Which leads us, inevitably, to the one character in this novel who has made peace with that economic reality — who has turned it into a philosophy and a strategy.
Jasper Milvain doesn't suffer from the literary market — he has mastered it, and next we ask whether that mastery is genius, cynicism, or something more unsettling still.

segments.title: Milvain's Ascent: The Ruthless Logic of Literary Success

utterances.text: We've been laughing — and wincing — at the desperate comedy of literary failure.
But Gissing gives us the equal and opposite case: a man for whom the literary market holds no terror whatsoever.
Jasper Milvain — charming, clear-eyed, utterly without illusion — and, it must be said, utterly without scruple.
The extraordinary thing about Jasper is that he announces himself on the very first page of the novel.
He tells his sisters, without the slightest embarrassment, that he intends to succeed by writing what the market wants — not what he believes in.
There's a line early on — he's speaking to Maud and Dora over breakfast — and he says something like:
"The chance of the market is everything. A lucky hit — and you're made."
And he means it entirely without irony — which is what makes him so remarkable, and so unsettling.
Gissing has created a character who is essentially saying the quiet part loud — loudly, cheerfully, over kedgeree.
And that cheerfulness is absolutely the key to Jasper as a literary creation.
Because what Gissing is showing us is a man who has perfectly internalised the logic of the literary commodity market.
Jasper doesn't experience alienation from his own labour — he's simply abolished the distinction between his authentic self and his marketable self.
He tells Reardon, in one of the novel's most devastating exchanges, that literature is a trade like any other.
"Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic accident, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman."
That formulation — 'cosmic accident' — is doing enormous work.
Jasper is not denying that genius exists — he's simply classifying it as irrelevant to the practical business of making a literary career.
I want to resist the temptation to read Jasper simply as Gissing's diagnosis of a corrupt system.
Because if we do that, we flatten him — we make him a mouthpiece rather than a person.
What strikes me about Jasper is the moral coherence of his position, taken on its own terms.
He is honest — bracingly, almost savagely honest — about what he wants and how he intends to get it.
And his treatment of his sisters — ensuring they have income, introducing them to the right people — shows a genuine, if unsentimental, loyalty.
The failure of character I see in Jasper is not cynicism — it is the absence of any love for the thing itself.
He has no devotion to literature as literature — and that, for me, is the quiet tragedy at the heart of his success.
Edmund, that's beautifully put — and I half agree.
But I think Gissing complicates it by showing us that Jasper is genuinely good company — genuinely engaging to read about.
His conversations with Reardon are among the best things in the book — the two men genuinely like each other, even as they represent utterly opposed philosophies.
And Jasper's advice to Reardon — write shorter, write simpler, stop worrying about posterity — is not wrong, exactly.
It's brutally practical in a way that Reardon's idealism simply cannot accommodate.
The comedy — if we can call it that — is that Jasper is giving excellent advice to a man constitutionally incapable of taking it.
Oliver's right that the friendship is genuine — Gissing is too good a novelist to make it simple.
But I think what makes Jasper's ascent so structurally important is the marriage plot.
His pursuit of Amy — and his eventual success in marrying her after Reardon's death — is not just romantic opportunism.
It is the novel's clearest demonstration that social capital, money, and literary reputation are all the same currency.
Amy comes to Jasper with an inheritance — and what does Jasper bring? Access, visibility, the right name in the right journals.
It's a perfectly rational exchange — which is precisely what makes it so cold to witness.
And Gissing closes the novel with Jasper and Amy at the top — comfortable, successful, and somehow smaller than everyone who failed.
That final image is where Gissing's moral imagination is at its most searching, I think.
Because Jasper has won — by every measurable standard, he has won.
And yet the novel does not celebrate him — it simply watches him, with a kind of cool, undeceived attention.
Gissing understood, I think, that the greatest condemnation of a man is not rage but description.
You simply show us Jasper at his breakfast table, writing his facile journalism, dining with the right editors — and the reader does the rest.
There's something in that technique that is closer to Trollope than to Dickens — a refusal of melodrama that is itself a moral stance.
And what I find perpetually delightful — and discomfiting — is that Jasper knows exactly what he is.
He doesn't deceive himself for a single moment — which is more than we can say for most of Gissing's characters, bless them.
There's that wonderful moment where he reflects — essentially out loud, with no shame — that a man of his abilities should not be wasting them on anything less than the most lucrative literary forms.
He is his own press agent, his own strategist, his own brand — decades before any of that vocabulary existed.
Gissing created the prototype of the modern literary careerist — and dressed him in a frock coat and had him call at Mudie's.
Jasper Milvain — the man who wins the game by understanding it's a game.
And yet there is one figure in this novel who understands the game just as clearly as Jasper — and is utterly destroyed by that understanding.
Marian Yule — brilliant, trapped, and too clear-eyed for her own comfort — is waiting for us in our next discussion.

segments.title: Marian's Silence: Trapped Between Intellect and Circumstance

utterances.text: We've been tracking Milvain's ruthless upward trajectory — his ability to sell himself, to convert talent into capital.
But New Grub Street places directly against that ascent one of its most haunting figures: Marian Yule.
Where Milvain speaks constantly and to great effect, Marian is defined by what she cannot say — and what the world will not hear.
Marian is one of the great quiet catastrophes of Victorian fiction, and I mean that as the highest possible praise.
Gissing gives her intelligence — genuine, formidable intelligence — and then proceeds to bury it alive, chapter by chapter.
The British Museum Reading Room scenes are extraordinary precisely because Gissing renders the institution itself as a kind of slow suffocation.
He describes the dome above her as something vast and indifferent — and Marian sits beneath it doing her father's hack-work while her own mind rots quietly on the vine.
There's a line — and I find it almost unbearable — where she reflects that the Reading Room catalogue might as well stand for the sum of all futility.
She thinks of all those thousands of volumes, all those strivings of human brains, and asks what it has ever amounted to.
That is Gissing landing a blow with a velvet glove — it reads like melancholy and it IS melancholy, but it's also a radical indictment of the entire literary enterprise.
I think one must be careful, however, not to read Marian purely as a victim of circumstance.
Gissing is far too scrupulous a novelist to let any of his characters off so easily.
Marian suffers, yes — but she also makes choices, or rather, she is defined by her failures of will at crucial moments.
Her relationship with Jasper Milvain is particularly instructive in this regard.
She sees him with admirable clarity — she knows what he is — and yet she permits herself to love him.
Gissing gives her a moment of quite devastating self-knowledge: she understands that Jasper values her chiefly for the prospect of her uncle's legacy.
And yet she holds to the attachment — not from blindness, but from something Gissing treats with great seriousness, which is the human unwillingness to surrender a hope.
That, to my mind, is a moral portrait, not a sociological diagram.
I don't dispute the moral portrait — but I'd ask what conditions make that particular failure of will so crushingly inevitable.
Marian is trapped in what we might call a double enclosure.
First, there is her father — Alfred Yule is one of Gissing's most savage portraits of literary labour devouring the domestic sphere.
He treats Marian not as a daughter but as an unpaid research assistant — her intellect is entirely at his disposal.
Second, the only escape route the culture offers her is marriage — and marriage, as Gissing anatomises it, is itself another form of economic dependency.
So when she latches onto the hope of Jasper, it isn't simply a failure of discernment — it is the only door she can see in the room.
Gissing has her reflect, with tremendous bitterness, that a woman of her position and her learning has nowhere to take either.
Her education is not capital — it is a burden, because the market has no use for it and no husband will be improved by it.
And what's so painful from a performer's perspective is the quality of her silence throughout the novel.
We never get Marian declaiming her situation — we get her observing it, almost numbly, from a slight remove.
There's a passage in Chapter 9 — it's in the Reading Room — where she looks up from the work she's doing for her father and the prose simply registers her exhaustion.
Not dramatised exhaustion — not Dickensian collapse — just the grey, factual weight of it.
Gissing writes, and I think this is verbatim: 'The fog of mind that results from long drudgery at uncongenial tasks had settled upon her.'
'Uncongenial tasks.' Two words that do more work than most novelists manage in a chapter.
That is beautifully observed, and I'd connect it to something Gissing does consistently with Marian that distinguishes her from his other suffering characters.
He never sentimentalises her.
Amy Reardon, in her way, can become almost theatrical in her suffering — there is a performance of middle-class distress in her chapters.
But Marian's suffering is rendered in a lower register — precise, affectless, almost clinical.
Which is why the moment the legacy is lost — when her uncle's money disappears and with it Jasper's interest — lands so very heavily.
Gissing offers almost no outburst, no scene of lamentation.
Just the quiet, terrible notation that she understood perfectly well what she had lost, and what she had been to Jasper all along.
That moment is structurally central to the whole novel's argument, I'd contend.
Because what Gissing is showing is that sentiment — love, attachment, hope — is not immune from economic logic.
The moment the money vanishes, the relationship evaporates — and Gissing renders this not as Jasper's individual villainy but as a systemic inevitability.
Jasper isn't monstrous — he's rational, by the novel's own logic.
And that is precisely what makes Marian's fate so devastating — she is defeated not by a villain but by a system that produces men like Jasper as its perfectly adapted specimens.
Gissing explicitly connects her situation to the larger literary marketplace — she cannot sell her own writing, she has no platform, she has no patron.
She is, in the most precise sense, surplus labour in a market that has already decided what it wants — and she is not it.
I'd just add — because I don't want to leave Marian entirely in the sociological frame, much as Daniel earns his argument — that Gissing gives her one extraordinary act of authorship.
Her letters to Jasper are the most alive prose she produces in the entire novel.
And there's a terrible irony in that — the one genre she can fully inhabit, she can write with warmth and intelligence and personality, is the private letter.
A form that earns no money, reaches no public, and in the end is not even preserved by its recipient.
Marian's silence, then, is not passive — it's the shape of a life that has been steadily denied the conditions for speech.
That conversation between form and meaning — between what Gissing shows us and how he chooses to show it — brings us naturally to the question of technique itself.
What kind of novelist is Gissing, and what does his narrative machinery reveal about his moral vision?

segments.title: The Narrative Game: Gissing's Technique and Moral Vision

utterances.text: We've been sitting with Marian's silence — that terrible gap between what she thinks and what she's permitted to say or do.
That leads us, I think, to a larger question about Gissing himself — not just what he shows us, but how he chooses to show it.
His narrative technique — the distance he keeps, the irony he deploys, the way he withholds sympathy at precisely the moment you most want it — is one of the most distinctive things about this novel.
Oliver, you've read more novels aloud than almost anyone — what does Gissing's prose actually feel like from the inside?
It feels, honestly, like being watched.
Most Victorian novelists — even the grimmer ones — give you warmth somewhere, a little authorial arm around the shoulder.
Gissing watches his characters the way a very intelligent, very tired man watches people missing their trains.
There's compassion there — deep compassion — but it's delivered through absolute clarity, not consolation.
Think of Edwin Reardon sitting in his flat in Regent's Park, trying to write his three volumes and producing nothing worth the paper.
Gissing doesn't rescue him even in the prose — the sentences themselves have that grinding, reluctant forward motion.
You feel the difficulty of composition in the act of reading.
That is well observed, and I'd go further.
Gissing's narrative distance is a moral instrument, not merely an aesthetic one.
He refuses to editorialize in the manner of, say, Thackeray — who can't resist stepping forward to tell you what to think.
In New Grub Street, you are made to form your own judgment — and that is a form of respect, I think.
Consider Jasper Milvain — the novel never quite condemns him outright.
He is charming, candid about his own ambitions, and ultimately successful.
The reader is invited to weigh Jasper's vitality against Reardon's integrity — and Gissing makes that weighing genuinely difficult.
That difficulty is the novel's moral seriousness.
I agree that the technique is remarkable, though I'd name what it does rather differently.
Gissing's irony is the irony of a man who understands the system from inside the machine room.
He doesn't withhold sympathy capriciously — he withholds it because he knows sympathy alone changes nothing.

The famous opening lines of the novel establish this immediately — Jasper Milvain, eating breakfast, announcing that Reardon is the kind of man who can't survive, as matter-of-factly as discussing the weather.
Gissing gives Jasper that speech because he wants us to hear how the market talks about human beings.
Not with cruelty — with breezy, breakfast-table certainty.
That opening is devastating when you read it aloud, actually.
Jasper says something very close to: 'literature nowadays is a trade.'
'Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic accident, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman.'
And he says it with complete cheerfulness — over the rashers, over the tea.
The performer's job is to resist making him villainous — because the horror is precisely that he isn't.
He's just rational.
And there, I think, is where Gissing most resembles the classical moralists he admired.
Johnson understood that a man could be intelligent and worldly and still choose badly.
Jasper doesn't choose badly by the world's measure — he chooses brilliantly.
But Gissing places beside him this exhausted, high-minded failure in Reardon — and asks you which life you actually admire.
Reardon's tragedy is not that he lacks talent — he has real gifts, as the novel makes plain in describing his earlier successes.
His tragedy is that he cannot make his talent function under commercial pressure.
That is a study in character, not a study in capitalism.
With respect, Sir Edmund, I think that distinction may be a false one here.
The commercial pressure is not background noise — it is the specific historical form that Reardon's weakness takes.
Take Harold Biffen — arguably the purest artist in the novel, writing his realist masterpiece 'Mr Bailey, Grocer.'
Biffen's project is to render ordinary life with absolute fidelity — no plot contrivances, no moral uplift for the lending libraries.
And what does that project earn him?
Poverty, obscurity, and finally — because his love for Amy's friend Reardon's world is also foreclosed — suicide.
The market doesn't destroy weak characters — it destroys the most honest ones.
Biffen is the character I find most heartbreaking, I'll confess.
Because he's not a self-deceiver — he knows exactly what he's doing and exactly what it costs.
There's a wonderful scene where he talks about his artistic creed — that the novel should represent life as it is lived by people the libraries never want to read about.
He describes it as the work of a man who respects his subjects too much to make them amusing.
That is a sentence Gissing couldn't have written without absolute conviction.
He is ventriloquizing his own artistic conscience through a man he then destroys.
One must also account for Amy Reardon in any discussion of the novel's moral vision.
She is often treated as a villain — the cold wife who abandons her husband in his hour of need.
But Gissing is far too honest a novelist for that.
He shows us Amy's genuine admiration for Edwin — and her equally genuine inability to inhabit permanent poverty with serenity.
She married someone she believed would rise — and he doesn't rise.
The novel asks whether that is weakness or simple honesty — and it does not answer cleanly.
That refusal to answer cleanly is, I submit, the sign of a morally serious novelist.
Amy's position is also a structural one, not merely a personal one.
A woman in her position has no income, no independent standing, and a child.
When Edwin can no longer provide, she faces a social and material crisis, not just an emotional one.
Gissing understood that the marriage plot in Victorian fiction was always also an economic plot.
And he refused to let sentiment obscure that arithmetic.
There's something Gissing does technically that I don't think gets enough attention — his chapter endings.
He almost never ends on a dramatic event — he ends on a mood, a weariness, a sentence that trails into silence.
It's the opposite of the Victorian cliffhanger — it's the anti-cliffhanger.
He ends chapters the way bad days end — not with explosion but with exhaustion.
And that is a formal choice that embodies the whole world of the novel.
Formal exhaustion as moral statement — that's a phrase I want to keep.
Gissing seems to be building a world where technique and subject matter are inseparable — the style performs the trap it describes.
Which brings us, I think, to the question we've been circling: what happens to the people caught inside that trap when talent and class and circumstance all converge at once?
That's exactly where we're going next — the impossible choices facing Gissing's characters when every exit is already closed.

segments.title: No Exit: Class, Talent, and the Impossible Choice

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Gissing controls our sympathies through technique — but technique always serves something deeper.
And what it serves, in this novel, is a vision of talent trapped — of people who can see exactly what the world is doing to them and cannot escape it.
That's where I'd like to end: with class, with talent, and with the question of whether Gissing's world allows any exit at all.
The novel's central cruelty is precisely that it gives its characters enough intelligence to understand their position — but not enough capital to change it.
Edwin Reardon is the perfect case.
He knows exactly what the literary market demands.
He knows it demands length, sensation, productivity on a commercial schedule — and he knows he cannot provide it without destroying what makes him a writer at all.
That's not a personal failing. That is the market consuming a sensibility it cannot use and discarding what it cannot price.
Gissing understood that the literary economy of the 1880s had produced a new kind of casualty — the educated man with no inherited wealth, whose only asset was taste.
And Reardon knows it — that's the unbearable thing.
There's that devastating moment — I think it's in the middle section — where he reflects that he has become a manufacturer of pages rather than a maker of books.
Gissing gives him the language to diagnose his own destruction with perfect clarity.
As a performer, I find that almost unbearably moving — the character who can articulate exactly how he is being ruined, sentence by sentence.
It's like watching a man drown who can name every current pulling him under.
I want to resist, gently, the idea that Reardon is purely a victim of economic forces.
Gissing is too honest a novelist to let him off so easily.
Reardon made choices — he married Amy, he retreated into his study, he refused the compromises that dozens of his contemporaries accepted without apparent self-destruction.

What Gissing is examining, I think, is not the cruelty of the market alone but something older — the question of whether a man of genuine artistic scruple can survive in any age that does not value scruple.
Johnson knew this predicament.
Grub Street itself knew it.
What Gissing adds is the Victorian marriage — Amy becomes, I'm afraid, the proximate instrument of Reardon's collapse quite as much as any publisher.
I won't quarrel with Amy as an instrument — but I'd say she is herself a victim of the same system, not its engineer.
Amy has been formed by a class that taught her to measure a man's worth in income.
She didn't invent those values. She absorbed them — as all of us absorb the values of the class that made us.
And then there is Jasper Milvain — who is the novel's most uncomfortable figure precisely because he has no illusions at all.
He states openly, almost gleefully, that he writes for the market, that he cultivates the right people, that literature is a trade and he intends to prosper at it.
And he does prosper. Which is Gissing's most savage structural joke.
Milvain is the one character in the novel who is genuinely fun to read aloud — and that's Gissing being extraordinarily clever.
He practically bounces off the page.
He's witty, he's candid, he's socially adroit — you can't help liking him even as you recognise exactly what he represents.

That line early in the novel — where he tells his sister that the difference between him and Reardon is simply that Reardon won't do what the age demands — is chilling because it is completely correct.
Milvain sees the game with perfect clarity and simply chooses to play it.
And Reardon sees it with equal clarity — and cannot.
That parallelism is the spine of the book, isn't it.
Gissing has constructed a kind of moral triptych — Reardon the conscientious failure, Milvain the cheerful careerist, and then Harold Biffen somewhere beneath them both.
Biffen is, in many ways, the novel's most heroic figure — and its most defeated.
He labours for years on his novel — Mr. Bailey, Grocer — a work of absolute artistic integrity that nobody wants and that the world will not receive.
His death — alone, by his own hand, having placed the manuscript carefully aside first — is the novel's quietest and most annihilating moment.
Gissing asks us to consider what it means that a man of that quality, that seriousness, finds no purchase in the world at all.
And the manuscript placed aside — that detail is almost unbearable.
It means Biffen still believed in the work even when he had ceased to believe in any future for himself.
The labour outlives the labourer — but to no purpose the market will recognise.
That is Gissing's answer to the question of whether talent is rewarded: sometimes it is immortalised in a manuscript that no one reads, in a garret that no one visits.
The system doesn't destroy talent loudly — it simply makes talent irrelevant.
What I keep coming back to, as a reader and as someone who has given voice to dozens of Victorian novels, is how modern this book feels.
Gissing was writing about a world in which culture had become content — in which the question was no longer what is good but what will sell.
And you feel throughout the novel — especially in Reardon's tortured relationship with his own work — the horror of a sensibility that cannot be switched off.
He cannot write badly enough, cheerfully enough, quickly enough — because some part of him refuses.
That refusal is both his integrity and his death sentence.
And yet — I want to end on this — Gissing does not write the novel in despair.
There is something in the very precision of his prose, the care with which he renders each life, that insists on the value of what he is describing even as the world he describes denies it.
The novel itself is Biffen's vindication in a sense — the serious work of art that the story says cannot exist, demonstrating by its own existence that it can.
That is not a small achievement. That is what serious literature does when it is working at its best.
I think that's precisely the right note to end on — and it speaks to why this novel, despite everything it shows us about failure, is so alive.

We've covered a great deal of ground today — the literary marketplace as a machine for sorting talent and money, the separate tragedies of Reardon and Biffen, Amy's position, Milvain's extraordinary survival.
And throughout, the question of what Gissing's technique is actually doing — how he builds sympathy, how he builds irony, often in the same paragraph.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, to Sir Edmund Leigh, and to Dr. Daniel Rosen — three readers who have made this novel feel newly urgent.
And to all of you who have listened — thank you for spending this time with us, and with Gissing.
New Grub Street is a book that repays every hour you give it — and I hope today has made it a little harder to put down.

c1:p43.text:
‘To be sure! To be sure!’ exclaimed their brother. ‘You have no faith. But
      just understand the difference between a man like Reardon and a man like
      me. He is the old type of unpractical artist; I am the literary man of
      1882. He won’t make concessions, or rather, he can’t make them; he can’t
      supply the market. I—well, you may say that at present I do nothing;
      but that’s a great mistake, I am learning my business. Literature nowadays
      is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic
      force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman. He thinks
      first and foremost of the markets; when one kind of goods begins to go off
      slackly, he is ready with something new and appetising. He knows perfectly
      all the possible sources of income. Whatever he has to sell he’ll get
      payment for it from all sorts of various quarters; none of your
      unpractical selling for a lump sum to a middleman who will make six
      distinct profits. Now, look you: if I had been in Reardon’s place, I’d
      have made four hundred at least out of “The Optimist”; I should have gone
      shrewdly to work with magazines and newspapers and foreign publishers, and—all
      sorts of people. Reardon can’t do that kind of thing, he’s behind his age;
      he sells a manuscript as if he lived in Sam Johnson’s Grub Street. But our
      Grub Street of to-day is quite a different place: it is supplied with
      telegraphic communication, it knows what literary fare is in demand in
      every part of the world, its inhabitants are men of business, however
      seedy.’
c1:p43.summary: Jasper articulates his philosophy: literature is a business, not an art; successful writers are those who understand the market and supply it strategically. He contrasts Reardon's 'old' unpractical approach with his own 'new' commercial method, emphasizing that writers must exploit all sources of income, manipulate magazines and newspapers, and treat their work as marketable goods rather than selling manuscripts for a lump sum like Samuel Johnson's era.
c1:p43.best_quote: Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman.

c16:p1.text:
His position was illogical—one result of the moral weakness which
      was allied with his aesthetic sensibility. Putting aside the worthlessness
      of current reviewing, the critic of an isolated book has of course nothing
      to do with its author’s state of mind and body any more than with the
      condition of his purse. Reardon would have granted this, but he could not
      command his emotions. He was in passionate revolt against the base
      necessities which compelled him to put forth work in no way representing
      his healthy powers, his artistic criterion. Not he had written this book,
      but his accursed poverty. To assail him as the author was, in his feeling,
      to be guilty of brutal insult. When by ill-hap a notice in one of the
      daily papers came under his eyes, it made his blood boil with a fierceness
      of hatred only possible to him in a profoundly morbid condition; he could
      not steady his hand for half an hour after. Yet this particular critic
      only said what was quite true—that the novel contained not a single
      striking scene and not one living character; Reardon had expressed himself
      about it in almost identical terms. But he saw himself in the position of
      one sickly and all but destitute man against a relentless world, and every
      blow directed against him appeared dastardly. He could have cried
      ‘Coward!’ to the writer who wounded him.
c16:p1.summary: Reardon's position is logically flawed: he knows critics should judge the work, not his circumstances, yet his morbid psychology makes him interpret all criticism as personal assault, generating bitter rage.
c16:p1.best_quote: Not he had written this book, but his accursed poverty

matched_quotes.text: Gissing writes that Reardon's imagination had 'refused to work,' that he 'could not get a single sentence constructed.

c18:p95.text:
How clean and sweet everything was! It is often said, by people who are
      exquisitely ignorant of the matter, that cleanliness is a luxury within
      reach even of the poorest. Very far from that; only with the utmost
      difficulty, with wearisome exertion, with harassing sacrifice, can people
      who are pinched for money preserve a moderate purity in their persons and
      their surroundings. By painful degrees Amy had accustomed herself to
      compromises in this particular which in the early days of her married life
      would have seemed intensely disagreeable, if not revolting. A housewife
      who lives in the country, and has but a patch of back garden, or even a
      good-sized kitchen, can, if she thinks fit, take her place at the wash-tub
      and relieve her mind on laundry matters; but to the inhabitant of a
      miniature flat in the heart of London anything of that kind is out of the
      question.
c18:p95.summary: The narrator challenges conventional wisdom that cleanliness is accessible to the poor, explaining instead that maintaining basic hygiene requires exhausting effort and sacrifice for those on limited means, and that Amy has gradually learned the painful compromises this entails.
c18:p95.best_quote: cleanliness is a luxury within reach even of the poorest. Very far from that; only with the utmost difficulty, with wearisome exertion, with harassing sacrifice, can people who are pinched for money preserve a moderate purity in their persons and their surroundings.

matched_quotes.text: Gissing writes of her with this devastating clarity: that she had 'the kind of nature which, in a woman, is seen at its best amid comfortable surroundings.

c21:p32.text:
‘Well, whether you’ve much to do with them or little, that’s how it was.
      And nicely she’s paid me out, has your niece, Miss Rudd. Of all the
      trouble I ever had with a girl! And now when she’s run away back ‘ome, and
      when I take the trouble to go arfter her, I’m to be insulted and abused as
      never was! Oh, they’re a nice respectable family, those Rudds! Mrs Rudd—that’s
      Mrs Yule’s sister—what a nice, polite-spoken lady she is, to be
      sure? If I was to repeat the language—but there, I wouldn’t lower
      myself. And I’ve been a brute of a mistress; I ill-use my servants, and I
      don’t give ‘em enough to eat, and I pay ‘em worse than any woman in
      London! That’s what I’ve learnt about myself by going to Perker Street,
      ‘Olloway. And when I come here to ask Mrs Yule what she means by
      recommending such a creature, from such a ‘ome, I get insulted by her
      gentleman husband.’
c21:p32.summary: Mrs Goby describes Annie's betrayal, the Rudds' rough treatment of her, and the damage to her reputation as a mistress, accusing Yule of complicity through his wife's recommendation.
c21:p32.best_quote: I've learnt about myself by going to Perker Street, 'Olloway: that I'm a brute of a mistress; I ill-use my servants, and I don't give 'em enough to eat, and I pay 'em worse than any woman in London!

matched_quotes.text: She thinks of all those thousands of volumes, all those strivings of human brains, and asks what it has ever amounted to.

c17:p111.text:
‘I don’t understand how you could be so thoughtless and heartless. You
      knew that I was almost mad with anxiety at times. Surely, any woman must
      have had the impulse to give what help was in her power. How could you
      hesitate? Had you no suspicion of what a relief and encouragement it would
      be to me, if you said: “Yes, we must go and live in a simpler way?” If
      only as a proof that you loved me, how I should have welcomed that! You
      helped me in nothing. You threw all the responsibility upon me—always
      bearing in mind, I suppose, that there was a refuge for you. Even now, I
      despise myself for saying such things of you, though I know so bitterly
      that they are true. It takes a long time to see you as such a different
      woman from the one I worshipped. In passion, I can fling out violent
      words, but they don’t yet answer to my actual feeling. It will be long
      enough yet before I think contemptuously of you. You know that when a
      light is suddenly extinguished, the image of it still shows before your
      eyes. But at last comes the darkness.’
c17:p111.summary: Reardon accuses Amy of offering no emotional support and expresses his slow realization that the woman he loved has become a stranger.
c17:p111.best_quote: You helped me in nothing. You threw all the responsibility upon me... It takes a long time to see you as such a different woman from the one I worshipped... But at last comes the darkness.

matched_quotes.text: Gissing writes, and I think this is verbatim: 'The fog of mind that results from long drudgery at uncongenial tasks had settled upon her.

c20:p48.text:
‘My husband is afraid Mr Reardon may fall seriously ill,’ said Mrs Carter.
      ‘And how dreadful! In such a place as that!’
c20:p48.summary: Jasper encounters Reardon on the street near the Yule house. Reardon's gaunt appearance and strange demeanor immediately concern him.
c20:p48.best_quote: Both stopped. Jasper held out his hand, but the other did not seem to notice it.

c7:p128.text:
In the meantime he married. Living in a garret, and supplying himself with
      the materials of his scanty meals, he was in the habit of making purchases
      at a little chandler’s shop, where he was waited upon by a young girl of
      no beauty, but, as it seemed to him, of amiable disposition. One holiday
      he met this girl as she was walking with a younger sister in the streets;
      he made her nearer acquaintance, and before long she consented to be his
      wife and share his garret. His brothers, John and Edmund, cried out that
      he had made an unpardonable fool of himself in marrying so much beneath
      him; that he might well have waited until his income improved. This was
      all very well, but they might just as reasonably have bidden him reject
      plain food because a few years hence he would be able to purchase
      luxuries; he could not do without nourishment of some sort, and the time
      had come when he could not do without a wife. Many a man with brains but
      no money has been compelled to the same step. Educated girls have a
      pronounced distaste for London garrets; not one in fifty thousand would
      share poverty with the brightest genius ever born. Seeing that marriage is
      so often indispensable to that very success which would enable a man of
      parts to mate equally, there is nothing for it but to look below one’s own
      level, and be grateful to the untaught woman who has pity on one’s
      loneliness.
c7:p128.summary: Alfred married the young girl from the chandler's shop where he lodged, despite his brothers' objections; the narrator defends this choice as practical necessity, given that educated women would not share poverty with a genius.
c7:p128.best_quote: Many a man with brains but no money has been compelled to the same step. Educated girls have a pronounced distaste for London garrets; not one in fifty thousand would share poverty with the brightest genius ever born.

c34:p49.text:
‘It comes to this, Marian,’ he said, with portentous gravity. ‘Support
      you, I could—I have little doubt of that. Maud is provided for, and
      Dora can make a living for herself. I could support you and leave you free
      to give your parents whatever you can earn by your own work. But—’
c34:p49.summary: Jasper explains that he could support Marian and allow her to aid her parents, but his career would suffer if he marries.
c34:p49.best_quote: Support you, I could—I have little doubt of that. Maud is provided for, and Dora can make a living for herself. I could support you and leave you free to give your parents whatever you can earn by your own work. But—

c16:p92.text:
He tore open the envelope. In delicacy Reardon and Biffen averted their
      eyes. There was silence for a minute, then a strange ejaculation from
      Whelpdale caused his friends to look up at him. He had gone pale, and was
      frowning at the sheet of paper which trembled in his hand.
c16:p92.summary: Whelpdale turns pale and trembles while reading the letter, his joy transformed instantly into shock and dismay.
c16:p92.best_quote: He had gone pale, and was frowning at the sheet of paper which trembled in his hand.

c16:p97.text:
‘She writes—that she has met an old lover—in Birmingham—that
      it was with him she had quarrelled-not with her father at all—that
      she ran away to annoy him and frighten him—that she has made it up
      again, and they’re going to be married!’
c16:p97.summary: Whelpdale reveals that his fiancée's letter explains she has reunited with an old lover in Birmingham and will marry him instead.
c16:p97.best_quote: She writes—that she has met an old lover—in Birmingham—that it was with him she had quarrelled-not with her father at all—that she ran away to annoy him and frighten him—that she has made it up again, and they're going to be married!

c10:p119.text:
‘I have thought of a new way of putting it. What I really aim at is an
      absolute realism in the sphere of the ignobly decent. The field, as I
      understand it, is a new one; I don’t know any writer who has treated
      ordinary vulgar life with fidelity and seriousness. Zola writes deliberate
      tragedies; his vilest figures become heroic from the place they fill in a
      strongly imagined drama. I want to deal with the essentially unheroic,
      with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the
      mercy of paltry circumstance. Dickens understood the possibility of such
      work, but his tendency to melodrama on the one hand, and his humour on the
      other, prevented him from thinking of it. An instance, now. As I came
      along by Regent’s Park half an hour ago a man and a girl were walking
      close in front of me, love-making; I passed them slowly and heard a good
      deal of their talk—it was part of the situation that they should pay
      no heed to a stranger’s proximity. Now, such a love-scene as that has
      absolutely never been written down; it was entirely decent, yet vulgar to
      the nth power. Dickens would have made it ludicrous—a gross
      injustice. Other men who deal with low-class life would perhaps have
      preferred idealising it—an absurdity. For my own part, I am going to
      reproduce it verbatim, without one single impertinent suggestion of any
      point of view save that of honest reporting. The result will be something
      unutterably tedious. Precisely. That is the stamp of the ignobly decent
      life. If it were anything but tedious it would be untrue. I speak, of
      course, of its effect upon the ordinary reader.’
c10:p119.summary: Biffen expounds his theory of absolute realism applied to ordinary, vulgar life—rejecting both Zola's melodrama and Dickens's humor, insisting instead on verbatim reproduction of the tedious, unheroic reality of common people.
c10:p119.best_quote: I want to deal with the essentially unheroic, with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance

c3:p121.text:
‘... The evil of the time is the multiplication of ephemerides. Hence a
      demand for essays, descriptive articles, fragments of criticism, out of
      all proportion to the supply of even tolerable work. The men who have an
      aptitude for turning out this kind of thing in vast quantities are
      enlisted by every new periodical, with the result that their productions
      are ultimately watered down into worthlessness.... Well now, there’s
      Fadge. Years ago some of Fadge’s work was not without a certain—a
      certain conditional promise of—of comparative merit; but now his
      writing, in my opinion, is altogether beneath consideration; how Rackett
      could be so benighted as to give him The Study—especially after a
      man like Henry Hawkridge—passes my comprehension. Did you read a
      paper of his, a few months back, in The Wayside, a preposterous
      rehabilitation of Elkanah Settle? Ha! Ha! That’s what such men are driven
      to. Elkanah Settle! And he hadn’t even a competent acquaintance with his
      paltry subject. Will you credit that he twice or thrice referred to
      Settle’s reply to “Absalom and Achitophel” by the title of “Absalom
      Transposed,” when every schoolgirl knows that the thing was called
      “Achitophel Transposed”! This was monstrous enough, but there was
      something still more contemptible. He positively, I assure you, attributed
      the play of “Epsom Wells” to Crowne! I should have presumed that every
      student of even the most trivial primer of literature was aware that
      “Epsom Wells” was written by Shadwell.... Now, if one were to take
      Shadwell for the subject of a paper, one might very well show how unjustly
      his name has fallen into contempt. It has often occurred to me to do this.
      “But Shadwell never deviates into sense.” The sneer, in my opinion, is
      entirely unmerited. For my own part, I put Shadwell very high among the
      dramatists of his time, and I think I could show that his absolute worth
      is by no means inconsiderable. Shadwell has distinct vigour of dramatic
      conception; his dialogue....’
c3:p121.summary: Alfred launches into a passionate critique of modern literary journalism: too many periodicals demand mediocre content; Fadge exemplifies declining standards through scholarly errors; yet Shadwell deserves reconsideration as a neglected dramatist.
c3:p121.best_quote: The evil of the time is the multiplication of ephemerides. Hence a demand for essays, descriptive articles, fragments of criticism, out of all proportion to the supply of even tolerable work.

c14:p155.text:
It was within his reach to marry a woman who would bring him wealth. He
      had that in mind; she understood it too well. But not one moment’s
      advantage would she relinquish. He must choose her in her poverty, and be
      content with what his talents could earn for him. Her love gave her the
      right to demand this sacrifice; let him ask for her love, and the
      sacrifice would no longer seem one, so passionately would she reward him.
c14:p155.summary: Marian insists that Jasper must choose her despite her lack of wealth, and that her love will compensate for any economic sacrifice. She believes her passion gives her the right to make this demand.
c14:p155.best_quote: He must choose her in her poverty, and be content with what his talents could earn for him. Her love gave her the right to demand this sacrifice; let him ask for her love, and the sacrifice would no longer seem one, so passionately would she reward him.

c15:p93.text:
‘Darling, they do struggle. But it’s as if an ever-increasing weight were
      round their necks; it drags them lower and lower. The world has no pity on
      a man who can’t do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be
      a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn’t take pity on you you will
      starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate. I have no
      right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it’s my own fault (in a sense)
      that I can’t continue as well as I began; if I could write books as good
      as the early ones I should earn money. For all that, it’s hard that I must
      be kicked aside as worthless just because I don’t know a trade.’
c15:p93.summary: Reardon argues that despite the efforts of struggling men with families, an ever-increasing burden drags them down; society is indifferent to human worth and offers no mercy to those without marketable skills; he accepts some personal responsibility but indicts the system as cruel and blind.
c15:p93.best_quote: The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn't take pity on you you will starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate.
